CHAPTER 6: THE FIRM

THE ROLE OF FIRMS IN AN ECONOMY
- Firms supply goods and services consumers want (food, medicine, clothing, games), provide employment, generate tax revenue and increase national income.
- Firms invest in research and development (R&D) to improve products (e.g. phones, gaming consoles, medical drugs).
- Incentives influence firms, e.g. high taxes on fossil fuels have incentivised car makers to invest in electric vehicles (EVs).

EFFICIENCY
- Efficient firms keep costs of production to a minimum and generally make higher profits.
- Inefficient firms with high costs tend to make less profit, or even make losses and have to close down.

TYPES OF COSTS
- Explicit costs: the monetary costs (expenses) of running a business that can be accounted for, e.g. wages, raw materials, insurance, energy costs. This chapter mainly deals with explicit costs.
- Implicit costs: non-monetary costs that are not accounted for in the same way as explicit costs.
- Implicit cost example 1: the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur's time - they could have earned money working for someone else.
- Implicit cost example 2: a shop owner who runs the business from premises they own could have earned 1,000 euro per week renting it out. This 1,000 euro foregone is an opportunity cost (implicit cost) and does not appear in the business accounts.
- Private costs: the costs borne by the individual who engages in the activity. Example: a smoker paying a 60 euro doctor's fee for a smoking-related illness.
- Social costs: the total costs to society of an activity, i.e. private costs PLUS external costs. Example for smoking: the private costs to the smoker, the cost of cleaning up cigarette litter, and the cost to the healthcare system of treating the smoker in hospital.

SHORT RUN VS LONG RUN
- Short run: a period of time in which at least one factor of production is fixed.
- Long run: a period of time in which all factors of production can be varied.
- Strawberry farmer example: she provides enterprise, uses land (fields), labour (strawberry pickers) and capital (a tractor).
- Within one season she can easily change how much land she uses and how many pickers she hires - these factors are variable.
- Getting a second tractor must be ordered and transported, which could take a full season - so capital is fixed.
- Her short run is up to the end of one season. Her long run is longer than one season, when all factors can be changed.
- Short and long run differ for every firm.

THE COSTS OF PRODUCTION (TABLE 6.2)
- Table 6.2 (fixed costs 50 euro): Quantity / FC / VC / TC / MC / AFC / AVC / ATC
- 0: 50 / 0 / 50 / - / - / - / -
- 1: 50 / 20 / 70 / 20 / 50 / 20 / 70
- 2: 50 / 35 / 85 / 15 / 25 / 17.5 / 42.5
- 3: 50 / 55 / 105 / 20 / 16.66 / 18.33 / 35
- 4: 50 / 76 / 126 / 21 / 12.50 / 19 / 31.5
- 5: 50 / 105 / 155 / 29 / 10 / 21 / 31
- 6: 50 / 135 / 185 / 30 / 8.33 / 22.5 / 30.83
- 7: 50 / 175 / 225 / 40 / 7.14 / 25 / 32.14
- 8: 50 / 230 / 280 / 55 / 6.25 / 28.75 / 35

FIXED COSTS (FC)
- Fixed costs: costs that do not vary with output. They must be paid whether zero or many units are produced.
- In Table 6.2, fixed costs are 50 euro.
- Examples: rent, insurance, commercial rates.
- Covid-19: in 2020 closed publicans still had to pay rent.
- Diagram in words: the FC curve is a horizontal straight line (at 50 euro in the example) - it stays the same at every quantity.

VARIABLE COSTS (VC)
- Variable costs: costs that vary with output. The more produced, the higher the variable costs.
- Examples: energy costs, wages of staff, raw materials.
- Diagram in words: the VC curve starts at zero (the origin) and rises upward as quantity rises, getting steeper.

TOTAL COSTS (TC)
- Total costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs.
- Diagram in words: the TC curve starts at the level of fixed costs (not at zero) and rises with output; it has the same shape as VC but is shifted up by the fixed costs.

MARGINAL COST (MC)
- Marginal cost: the extra cost of producing an extra unit of output.
- Formula: MC = change in total cost / change in quantity.
- Example: going from 3 to 4 units, TC rises from 105 euro to 126 euro, so MC = 21 euro.
- Shape: the MC curve is shaped like the Nike symbol (a 'tick') - it falls slightly at first, then rises steeply.

AVERAGE FIXED COST (AFC)
- Average fixed cost: fixed cost per unit. AFC = Fixed cost / Quantity.
- Example: at 4 units, AFC = 12.50 euro per unit.
- Shape: AFC falls steeply at first and then appears to level off, because fixed costs are spread over a larger quantity. E.g. from 1 to 2 units AFC halves from 50 euro to 25 euro.

AVERAGE VARIABLE COST (AVC)
- Average variable cost: variable cost per unit. AVC = Variable cost / Quantity.
- Example: at 4 units, AVC = 19 euro per unit.
- Shape: AVC is low at first, then rises as output expands, due to the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns (Chapter 9). It is U-shaped.

AVERAGE TOTAL COST (ATC), ALSO CALLED AVERAGE COST (AC)
- Average total cost: total cost per unit.
- Example: at 4 units, ATC = 31.50 euro per unit.
- Method 1: ATC = Total cost / Quantity, e.g. 126 / 4 = 31.50 euro.
- Method 2: ATC = AFC + AVC, e.g. 12.50 + 19 = 31.50 euro.
- Shape: U-shaped (explained in the SRAC section below).

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (TABLE 6.4)
- Total costs: 0 units = 100; 1 = 120; 2 = 130; 3 = 167; 4 = 190 euro.
- Fixed costs = 100 euro, because total cost is 100 euro when nothing is produced.
- Variable cost of 3 units = 167 - 100 = 67 euro.
- At 3 units: AFC = 100/3 = 33.33; AVC = 67/3 = 22.33; ATC = 167/3 = 55.66 euro.
- At 4 units: AFC = 100/4 = 25; AVC = 90/4 = 22.50; ATC = 190/4 = 47.50 euro.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (TABLE 6.5: AVC AND AFC)
- Quantity / AVC / AFC: 1: 120/240; 2: 80/120; 3: 88.33/80; 4: 110.5/60; 5: 150/48; 6: 200/40.
- ATC of 5 units = AFC + AVC = 48 + 150 = 198 euro.
- Fixed cost: AFC = FC / Q, so at 3 units 80 x 3 = 240 euro.
- Total cost of 3 units: ATC = 80 + 88.33 = 168.33; TC = 168.33 x 3 = 505 euro (rounding).
- Variable cost of 6 units: VC = AVC x Q = 200 x 6 = 1,200 euro.
- Rearranged: FC = AFC x Q; VC = AVC x Q; TC = ATC x Q.

RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN AVERAGE COST (AC) AND MARGINAL COST (MC)
- Class-age example: average age 17; a new student aged 20 raises it, aged 12 lowers it, aged 17 leaves it unchanged.
- When MC is below AC, AC is falling.
- When MC is above AC, AC is rising.
- When MC = AC, AC is at a minimum.
- Diagram in words: a U-shaped AC curve and a Nike-shaped MC curve; MC rises and cuts AC at the lowest point of the AC curve.

ECONOMIES OF SCALE
- KitKat example: the Nestle plant in York, UK makes 3 million bars a day; a TY mini-company in a Wexford school makes 20 bars a day. Nestle has the lower unit cost because of mass production and economies of scale.
- Economies of scale: the cost savings or lower costs per unit a firm enjoys when output increases.
- Internal economies of scale: forces within a firm that cause cost per unit to fall as the firm expands.
- External economies of scale: forces within an industry that cause cost per unit to fall for all firms in the industry as the industry expands.

INTERNAL ECONOMIES OF SCALE (EXAMPLES)
- 1. Purchasing economies (bulk buying discounts): the KitKat plant buys milk, cocoa and sugar in bulk and negotiates discounts; the TY students buy in a local shop and get no discount.
- 2. Specialisation of labour: hundreds of workers each focus on one task and become efficient; the two TY students do every task and waste time switching tasks.
- 3. Financial economies: Nestle can easily get low-interest bank loans because of its size and importance as a customer; TY students borrow from friends and family at high interest.
- 4. Automation/machinery: a large firm can afford assembly lines and machines, which are expensive to install but lower cost per unit.

EXTERNAL ECONOMIES OF SCALE (EXAMPLES)
- 1. Suppliers benefit too: York has had a chocolate industry since the 1700s. Local milk suppliers expanded, gained their own economies of scale and passed savings on, lowering raw material costs for all chocolate firms.
- 2. Access to skilled labour: local education centres provide courses (food production, marketing, quality control), lowering recruitment and training costs for all firms.
- 3. Improvement in infrastructure: local authorities provide roads, energy and water to growing industries, lowering costs for all firms.
- 4. Research and development: R&D by firms in an industry benefits all firms, e.g. a new assembly-line machine developed by one chocolate maker can be used by all.

DISECONOMIES OF SCALE
- Diseconomies of scale: the cost disadvantages or higher costs per unit as output increases.
- Internal diseconomies of scale: forces within a firm that cause cost per unit to rise as the firm expands.
- External diseconomies of scale: forces within an industry that cause cost per unit to rise as the industry expands.

INTERNAL DISECONOMIES (EXAMPLES)
- 1. Communication difficulties: Nestle employs 291,000 people globally and Cadbury 45,000. It is hard to communicate with all staff efficiently and in time.
- 2. Unproductive and unmotivated staff: workers who specialise in one narrow task get bored, lose motivation and productivity falls.
- 3. Management/administration costs: more workers need more managers, supervisors and an expensive HR department for staff administration and recruitment.

EXTERNAL DISECONOMIES (EXAMPLES)
- 1. Inadequate infrastructure: high demand for roads, ports, energy and water causes traffic jams, port delays and supply disruptions.
- 2. Raw material shortages: rising demand raises raw material prices and disrupts supply, e.g. global cocoa shortages have raised chocolate production costs.
- 3. Recruitment difficulties: rising demand for specialised staff causes labour shortages, forcing firms to pay higher wages to attract and retain workers.

SHORT RUN AVERAGE COST (SRAC) VS LONG RUN AVERAGE COST (LRAC)
- Both slope down then up, but for different reasons.
- SRAC has a deep U-shape. LRAC has a shallow U-shape.
- SRAC slopes down because fixed costs are spread over a greater quantity (falling AFC) and because of the benefits of specialisation of labour as more workers are hired.
- SRAC slopes up because of the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns; beyond a certain point bottlenecks occur, causing inefficiency and higher costs per unit.
- LRAC slopes down because economies of scale (internal and external) outweigh diseconomies as production first expands.
- LRAC slopes up because diseconomies of scale eventually outweigh economies of scale.

DERIVING THE LRAC CURVE
- Example: a manufacturer builds a new factory extension (capital) every month for six months; other factors can be changed weekly.
- Short run here = up to one month (capital fixed). Long run = beyond one month.
- Each factory size has its own SRAC curve (SRAC1 to SRAC6).
- A profit-maximising firm wants to produce at the minimum point of each SRAC.
- Joining the minimum points of all the SRAC curves gives the LRAC curve (Figure 6.18).

ECONOMIES OF SCALE AND THE SIZE OF FIRMS
- Where economies of scale are prevalent, firms are large and few - high market concentration, a less competitive market. Mass production savings can mean lower prices for consumers.
- Examples: mobile devices (Apple, Samsung, Huawei); cars (Ford, VW, Toyota, Renault, Honda, BMW, Opel); gaming consoles (PlayStation, Xbox).
- Where economies of scale are not prevalent, firms are small and many - low market concentration, a more competitive market. Examples: coffee shops, restaurants, pubs, hairdressers, nail bars, bakeries, butchers.
- Market concentration: how far a market is dominated by a small number of large suppliers.
- Economies of scale act as a barrier to entry (source of monopoly power) - see Chapter 8.

WHY SMALL FIRMS SURVIVE
- Ireland has around 250,000 small- to medium-sized enterprises employing around 1 million people.
- The market may be too small for a large business, e.g. a small village shop.
- Small firms give a more personal service, e.g. hairdressers, plumbers.
- Consumers are often loyal to small local firms owned by community members.
- Small firms work in niche markets, e.g. homemade bread, farmhouse cheeses.

CAN FIRMS BECOME TOO BIG?
- In 2020 the CEOs of Google (Alphabet), Apple, Facebook and Amazon appeared before the US Congress over concerns they were abusing dominant positions.
- Facebook was accused of eliminating competition by taking over rivals, giving it monopoly power in online marketing and social networking.
- Amazon hosts sellers while competing against them, and was accused of undercutting rivals to force them to sell.
- Google was accused of hiding rivals' search results; contracts making it the default search engine on some phones act as a barrier to entry.
- Apple: app sellers can only sell through the App Store and are charged 30% of their revenue (mid-2020). In 2020 Epic Games (Fortnite) offered a non-Apple payment option; Apple removed Fortnite from the App Store, leading to court proceedings.

ADVANTAGES OF LARGE FIRMS
- 1. Resources to invest in R&D; innovation (fitness watches, slimmer phones, earbuds, better consoles). Samsung and Apple constantly improve devices.
- 2. Economies of scale allow lower prices for consumers.
- 3. Job security for employees, as a new rival is unlikely to put the firm out of business.

DISADVANTAGES OF LARGE FIRMS
- 1. 'Too big to fail' leads to moral hazard. Irish banks lent recklessly during the Celtic Tiger, knowing the state would bail them out.
- Moral hazard: the lack of an incentive an individual or firm has to guard against risk when they are protected from the consequences of their actions.
- 2. Big firms can take over or merge with smaller rivals, or target their customers if refused, e.g. Amazon undercut diapers.com's prices until it had to sell.
- 3. Some big tech firms can influence political opinion, e.g. the Cambridge Analytica scandal showed Facebook was used to influence election results.
- 4. High market concentration makes collusion easier, e.g. price fixing, dividing up sales territories.
- 5. Firms with little competition can charge very high prices (e.g. Apple's App Store fee) or undercut rivals, then raise prices once rivals are gone.

REVENUE (TABLE 6.10, PRICE FIXED AT 20 EURO, PERFECT COMPETITION)
- Quantity / Price / TR / MR / AR / MC: 1: 20/20/20/20/15; 2: 20/40/20/20/13; 3: 20/60/20/20/16; 4: 20/80/20/20/20; 5: 20/100/20/20/25.
- Columns 1 and 2 form a demand schedule.
- Total revenue (TR) = Price x Quantity, e.g. 4 x 20 = 80 euro.
- Marginal revenue (MR): the extra revenue from supplying an extra unit. MR = change in TR / change in Q. From 2 to 3 units TR rises from 40 to 60, so MR = 20.
- In perfect competition MR = price.
- Average revenue (AR): revenue per unit. AR = TR / Quantity. In perfect competition AR = price.

PROFIT MAXIMISATION
- Most firms aim to maximise profits. A firm produces the quantity where MR = MC.
- Table 6.10: produce units 1-3 (MR 20 > MC of 15, 13, 16), unit 4 (MR 20 = MC 20); NOT unit 5 (MR 20 < MC 25), which makes a loss.
- Profit-maximising rule: produce the quantity where MR = MC and MC is rising; never produce beyond that point.
- Why 'where MR = MC' and not 'just before': if MR were 20 and MC 19.99 the unit should be made; it is awkward to say or draw 'just before', so we say 'where MR = MC'.
- Diagram in words (Figure 6.19): horizontal MR line at 20 euro; MC curve rising through it at quantity 4.

WORKED EXAMPLE (TABLES 6.11 AND 6.12, PRICE 10 EURO)
- Profit = TR - TC. TR = P x Q. MR = change in TR / change in Q. MC = change in TC / change in Q.
- Q / TR / TC / Profit / MR / MC: 0: 0/6/-6; 1: 10/16/-6/10/10; 2: 20/19/1/10/3; 3: 30/25/5/10/6; 4: 40/35/5/10/10; 5: 50/46/4/10/11; 6: 60/58/2/10/12; 7: 70/67/3/10/9.
- MR = MC at 4 units: the 4th unit adds 10 euro to TC and 10 euro to TR. Profit is 5 euro. (3 units also gives 5 euro profit but we say 'produce where MR = MC'.)
- MR = MC can happen twice (here at 1 unit and at 4 units). 1 unit is loss-making.
- Full profit-maximising condition: MR = MC AND MC cuts MR from below.
- Diagram in words (Figure 6.20): horizontal MR = AR line; Nike-shaped MC cuts it twice, first from above at Q1 (falling MC) then from below at Q2 (rising MC). Q2 is profit-maximising.

NORMAL PROFIT AND SUPERNORMAL PROFIT
- AR = revenue per unit; AC = cost per unit.
- In economics, average costs include a normal profit, so when AR = AC the firm is making a (normal) profit - not just 'breaking even' as in business or accounting.
- Table 6.13 breakdown of AC: energy 3 euro, labour 4 euro, raw materials 2 euro, normal profit 1 euro = AC of 10 euro.
- Normal profit is treated as a cost, like a bill that must be paid to the owner/entrepreneur.
- Normal profit: the profit earned when AR = AC. A firm must earn at least normal profit to stay in business in the long run.
- Supernormal profit: profit earned when AR is greater than AC (also called abnormal profit).
- Example: AC = 10 euro, AR = 12 euro. The owner earns normal profit of 1 euro and supernormal profit of 2 euro per unit.

AIMS OTHER THAN PROFIT MAXIMISATION
- Can be a feature of oligopoly markets (Chapter 8).
- Maximise market share (be the largest firm): charge unsustainably low prices, spend heavily on advertising or acquiring other firms. Not profitable in the short run, e.g. Amazon undercutting diapers.com.
- Avoid attracting new firms: large profits attract competition, so a firm may settle for lower profits.
- Satisfactory profit for a reasonable standard of living, e.g. a family-owned fuel garage owner who chooses not to open 24 hours to avoid the workload.
- Avoid unwanted attention: large profits may lead to higher taxes, regulation or price ceilings.
- Aim to be bought by another firm, e.g. WhatsApp was unprofitable until bought by Facebook.
- Social function: e.g. a charity such as Meals on Wheels; revenue matters but profit is not the main aim.

rows.prompt: Which of these is a role of firms in an economy?
options: Deciding the rate of income tax
Generating tax revenue for the government
rows.explanation: Firms generate tax revenue for the government, as well as providing jobs and goods.

rows.prompt: Which of these is an explicit cost?
options: Rent the owner could have earned
Income given up by the entrepreneur
rows.explanation: Explicit costs are monetary expenses that can be accounted for, such as wages.

rows.prompt: A shop owner uses her own premises instead of renting it out for 1,000 euro a week. The 1,000 euro is:
rows.explanation: It is an opportunity cost that does not appear in the accounts, so it is an implicit cost.

rows.prompt: Social costs are equal to:
rows.explanation: Social costs are the total costs to society, i.e. private costs and external costs.

rows.prompt: The short run is a period of time in which:
options: At least one factor of production is fixed
All factors of production can be varied
The firm earns only normal profit
Total costs are equal to zero
rows.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of the short run.

rows.prompt: For the strawberry farmer, which factor of production is fixed in the short run?
rows.explanation: A second tractor could take a full season to get, so capital is fixed.

rows.prompt: Total costs are calculated as:
rows.explanation: TC = FC + VC.

rows.prompt: Total cost rises from 105 euro to 126 euro when output goes from 3 to 4 units. The marginal cost is:
rows.explanation: MC is the change in total cost from one extra unit: 126 - 105 = 21 euro.

rows.prompt: Fixed costs are 50 euro. What is the average fixed cost when 4 units are made?
rows.explanation: AFC = FC / Q = 50 / 4 = 12.50 euro.

rows.prompt: Why does the AFC curve fall steeply and then level off?
options: Workers become bored and less productive
Fixed costs are spread over more units
rows.explanation: As output grows, the same fixed costs are spread over a larger quantity.

rows.prompt: The AVC curve eventually rises because of:
options: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns
rows.explanation: The chapter states variable cost per unit rises due to diminishing marginal returns.

rows.prompt: AFC is 12.50 euro and AVC is 19 euro. What is the average total cost?
rows.explanation: ATC = AFC + AVC = 12.50 + 19 = 31.50 euro.

rows.prompt: AVC is 200 euro when 6 units are produced. What is the variable cost?
rows.explanation: VC = AVC x Q = 200 x 6 = 1,200 euro.

rows.prompt: AFC is 80 euro when 3 units are produced. What are the fixed costs?
rows.explanation: FC = AFC x Q = 80 x 3 = 240 euro.

rows.prompt: When marginal cost is below average cost, average cost is:
rows.explanation: Like a younger student lowering the class's average age, a lower MC pulls AC down.

rows.prompt: The MC curve cuts the AC curve at:
options: The lowest point of the AC curve
The highest point of the AC curve
The point where output is zero
The point where AFC is highest
rows.explanation: When MC = AC, AC is at a minimum.

rows.prompt: Economies of scale are:
options: Higher costs per unit as output increases
Lower costs per unit as output increases
Extra revenue from one more unit sold
rows.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of economies of scale.

rows.prompt: Which of these is an INTERNAL economy of scale?
options: Local courses that train skilled workers
Better roads built for the industry
rows.explanation: Purchasing economies happen within the firm, so they are internal.

rows.prompt: Local milk suppliers grow and pass savings on to all York chocolate firms. This is:
rows.explanation: It lowers costs for all firms in the industry as the industry grows.

rows.prompt: Workers doing one narrow task become bored and less productive. This is:
rows.explanation: It is a force within the firm that raises cost per unit as it grows.

rows.prompt: Global cocoa shortages raising costs for all chocolate makers is an example of:
rows.explanation: Raw material shortages raise costs for every firm in the industry.

rows.prompt: Why does the LRAC curve slope upward eventually?
options: Fixed costs are spread over more units
Diseconomies of scale outweigh economies of scale
rows.explanation: Beyond a point, diseconomies of scale outweigh economies and LRAC rises.

rows.prompt: How is the LRAC curve derived?
options: By joining the minimum points of the SRAC curves
By adding AFC and AVC together
By joining the maximum points of the MC curves
By dividing total revenue by quantity
rows.explanation: Each factory size has its own SRAC; joining their lowest points gives the LRAC.

rows.prompt: Where economies of scale are prevalent, markets tend to have:
rows.explanation: Firms are large and few, so markets are less competitive.

rows.prompt: Moral hazard is:
options: The risk that a firm becomes too small to survive
Charging very low prices to force rivals out
Lack of incentive to guard against risk when protected from the consequences
Agreeing prices secretly with rival firms
rows.explanation: Irish banks lending recklessly during the Celtic Tiger is the chapter's example.

rows.prompt: Total revenue is calculated as:
rows.explanation: TR = P x Q, e.g. 20 x 4 = 80 euro.

rows.prompt: A profit-maximising firm produces the quantity where:
options: AR = AC and AC is falling
MR = MC and MC cuts MR from below
TR is at its highest point
MC is at its lowest point
rows.explanation: This rule avoids the loss-making point where MC cuts MR from above.

rows.prompt: Price is 20 euro. The MC of the 5th unit is 25 euro. Should the firm make it?
options: Yes, because total revenue still rises
Yes, because AR is equal to price
No, because fixed costs would rise
No, MR is less than MC so it makes a loss
rows.explanation: MR (20) < MC (25), so the 5th unit lowers profit.

rows.prompt: In economics, when AR = AC the firm is earning:
rows.explanation: AC includes normal profit, so AR = AC means normal profit is earned.

rows.prompt: AC is 10 euro (including 1 euro normal profit) and AR is 12 euro. Supernormal profit per unit is:
rows.explanation: Supernormal profit is AR - AC = 12 - 10 = 2 euro.

rows.prompt: WhatsApp was unprofitable until Facebook bought it. This shows a firm aiming to:
options: Earn a reasonable standard of living
rows.explanation: The owners made their profit only once the firm was bought.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between explicit costs and implicit costs, giving one example of each.
rows.model_answer: Explicit costs are monetary costs of running a business that appear in the accounts, such as wages or raw materials. Implicit costs are non-monetary costs not accounted for in the same way, such as the opportunity cost of the owner's time or the rent she could have earned on her own premises.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between the short run and the long run, using the strawberry farmer example.
rows.model_answer: The short run is a period when at least one factor of production is fixed; the long run is when all factors can be varied. The farmer can change land and pickers within a season, but getting a new tractor could take a full season, so her short run is up to one season and her long run is longer than one season.

rows.prompt: State two methods for calculating average total cost and use each for 4 units with TC 126 euro, AFC 12.50 euro and AVC 19 euro.
rows.model_answer: Method 1: ATC = TC / Q = 126 / 4 = 31.50 euro. Method 2: ATC = AFC + AVC = 12.50 + 19 = 31.50 euro.

rows.prompt: Describe the relationship between marginal cost and average cost.
rows.model_answer: When MC is below AC, AC is falling. When MC is above AC, AC is rising. When MC equals AC, AC is at its minimum, so the MC curve cuts the AC curve at its lowest point.

rows.prompt: Name two internal economies of scale and two external economies of scale.
rows.model_answer: Internal: purchasing economies (bulk-buying discounts) and specialisation of labour (also financial economies and automation). External: access to skilled labour from local training courses and improved infrastructure such as roads, energy and water (also supplier savings and shared R&D).

rows.prompt: Draw and label a short run average cost curve (describe it in words) and give one reason why it slopes down and one reason why it slopes up.
rows.model_answer: Costs on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis, with a deep U-shaped curve labelled SRAC. It slopes down because fixed costs are spread over more units and because of specialisation of labour. It slopes up because of the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns, as bottlenecks cause inefficiency.

rows.prompt: Give three reasons why small firms survive in the Irish economy.
rows.model_answer: The market may be too small for a large firm, e.g. a village shop. Small firms can give a more personal service, e.g. hairdressers and plumbers. Consumers are often loyal to local firms, and small firms can work in niche markets such as farmhouse cheese.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between normal profit and supernormal profit.
rows.model_answer: Normal profit is the profit earned when AR = AC; it is treated as a cost and is the minimum a firm needs to stay in business in the long run. Supernormal (abnormal) profit is profit earned when AR is greater than AC, i.e. profit above normal profit.

rows.prompt: A firm's total costs are: 0 units = 100 euro; 1 unit = 120 euro; 2 units = 130 euro; 3 units = 167 euro; 4 units = 190 euro. (i) State the fixed costs and explain your answer. (ii) Calculate the variable cost of 3 units. (iii) Calculate the AFC, AVC and ATC of producing 4 units. Show your workings. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) Fixed costs are 100 euro, because total cost is 100 euro when nothing is produced, and fixed costs must be paid whatever the output. (ii) VC = TC - FC = 167 - 100 = 67 euro. (iii) At 4 units: VC = 190 - 100 = 90 euro. AFC = FC / Q = 100 / 4 = 25 euro. AVC = VC / Q = 90 / 4 = 22.50 euro. ATC = TC / Q = 190 / 4 = 47.50 euro (check: 25 + 22.50 = 47.50 euro).
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 5 marks: figure 2m + explanation 3m. (ii) 5 marks: correct answer with workings 5m (formula 2m, answer 3m). (iii) 10 marks: AFC 3m, AVC 3m, ATC 4m (workings must be shown for full marks).

rows.prompt: Explain, using examples, the difference between internal and external economies of scale. Give two examples of each. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Internal economies of scale are forces within a firm that lower its cost per unit as the firm itself expands. 1. Purchasing economies: a large firm such as the Nestle KitKat plant buys milk, cocoa and sugar in bulk and negotiates discounts, unlike a small TY mini-company. 2. Specialisation of labour: hundreds of workers each focus on one task and become efficient, lowering cost per unit. External economies of scale are forces within an industry that lower cost per unit for all firms as the industry expands. 1. Access to skilled labour: in York, local education centres run courses in food production and quality control, lowering recruitment and training costs for all chocolate firms. 2. Improved infrastructure: local authorities provide roads, energy and water for a growing industry, lowering costs for every firm.
rows.marking_scheme: Definitions: internal 3m, external 3m (6m). Examples: 4 examples x 3.5m (1m statement + 2.5m explanation) = 14m. Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain, with the aid of diagrams, why the short run average cost (SRAC) curve and the long run average cost (LRAC) curve are both U-shaped, and explain how the LRAC curve is derived. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagrams (in words): costs on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal. The SRAC is a deep U-shape. The LRAC is a shallow U-shape drawn below a series of SRAC curves (SRAC1 to SRAC6) and touching their lowest points. SRAC slopes down because fixed costs are spread over a greater quantity, so AFC falls, and because specialisation of labour increases efficiency as more workers are hired. SRAC slopes up due to the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns: beyond a point bottlenecks occur, causing inefficiency and higher costs per unit. LRAC slopes down because internal and external economies of scale (e.g. bulk buying, specialisation, skilled labour) outweigh diseconomies as output first expands. LRAC slopes up because diseconomies of scale (e.g. communication difficulties, unmotivated staff, raw material shortages) eventually outweigh economies of scale. Derivation: each factory size has its own SRAC curve. A profit-maximising firm wants to produce at the minimum point of each SRAC. Joining the minimum points of all the SRAC curves gives the LRAC curve.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagrams: SRAC correctly labelled 3m; LRAC with SRACs correctly labelled 4m (7m). SRAC shape: 2 reasons x 3m (down and up) = 6m. LRAC shape: 2 reasons x 3m = 6m. Derivation of LRAC: 6m (each SRAC for a plant size 2m, minimum points 2m, joined 2m). Total 25 marks.

rows.prompt: A firm sells in a perfectly competitive market at a price of 10 euro. Its total costs are: 0 = 6; 1 = 16; 2 = 19; 3 = 25; 4 = 35; 5 = 46 euro. (i) Calculate total revenue, profit, MR and MC for each output level. (ii) State the profit-maximising rule and identify the profit-maximising output. (iii) Explain why MR = MC at one unit is not profit-maximising. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) TR = P x Q: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Profit = TR - TC: -6, -6, 1, 5, 5, 4. MR = change in TR = 10 for each unit. MC = change in TC: 10, 3, 6, 10, 11. (ii) A profit-maximising firm produces the quantity where MR = MC and MC cuts MR from below. This happens at 4 units, where MR = MC = 10 euro and profit is 5 euro. The 5th unit would not be produced as MC (11) is greater than MR (10). (iii) MR also equals MC at one unit, but there MC is falling and cuts MR from above; the firm makes a loss of 6 euro. So the condition that MC must cut MR from below (MC rising) is needed to find the true profit-maximising output.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 10m: TR 2m, profit 3m, MR 2m, MC 3m. (ii) 9m: rule stated 4m (MR = MC 2m + MC cutting from below 2m); output of 4 units 3m; reason for not producing 5th unit 2m. (iii) 6m: 2 points x 3m. Total 25 marks.

rows.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages for an economy of markets dominated by a small number of large firms. Refer to the technology industry in your answer. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Advantages: 1. Large firms have the resources for research and development and keep innovating, e.g. Samsung and Apple constantly improve their devices. 2. Economies of scale allow cost savings to be passed to consumers as lower prices. 3. Employees enjoy job security as a new rival is unlikely to put the firm out of business. Disadvantages: 1. Firms that are 'too big to fail' create moral hazard, as with Irish banks lending recklessly in the Celtic Tiger. 2. Big firms can take over rivals or undercut them, e.g. Amazon undercut diapers.com until it had to sell. 3. High concentration makes collusion such as price fixing easier, and firms can charge high prices, e.g. Apple's 30% App Store charge. 4. Some tech firms can influence political opinion, as shown in the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
rows.marking_scheme: 4 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation), at least one advantage and one disadvantage required. Total 20 marks.
